subChunks.title: Your First Documented Pedigree
subChunks.hookHtml: Every element of the Genealogy APPRENTICE tier has prepared you for this moment: choosing the right record, evaluating its information, citing it precisely, recording your searches, checking coherence, and placing each ancestor in their historical context. Now you bring these skills together into one documented pedigree — not a list of names, but a record of evidence.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What this capstone asks you to produce

Your task is to document three generations of your own (or an assigned) family — yourself, your parents, and your grandparents — using primary and secondary sources correctly identified and cited. The output is a completed pedigree chart and a family group sheet for one couple in the chart, with every fact sourced.

If you are using your own family, you will have access to personal knowledge and family documents. If you are assigned a historical family, you will be working entirely from archive sources. Both approaches test the same skills.

The four quality standards

Your pedigree will be assessed against four standards, each derived from skills developed in this tier:

  1. Source completeness: every date, place, and relationship must be supported by a cited source. A fact without a citation is not a fact — it is a claim.
  2. Information classification: for each cited source, identify whether the key information it provides is primary or secondary. Explain how this affects your confidence in the fact.
  3. Coherence: all dates and relationships must be internally consistent. No parent younger than their child; no overlapping birth intervals for the same mother; no death before a documented later event.
  4. Research log: provide a summary research log covering the sources you searched, what you found (or did not find), and the search terms used. Negative searches must be documented.

Citation format — the minimum standard

Every source citation should include:

  • Record type (e.g. England and Wales birth registration; US federal census; Roman Catholic baptism register)
  • Repository or database (e.g. General Register Office; FamilySearch; Ancestry; county record office)
  • Specific identifying information (year, registration district, volume and page; film number; parish name and register volume)
  • Date you accessed it (for online resources)

Example of an adequate citation: "England and Wales birth registration, June quarter 1872, Aston registration district, vol. 6d, p. 142 [for Patrick Walsh]; image viewed on Ancestry.com, 15 April 2024."

Example of an inadequate citation: "Ancestry.com" or "the internet."

What Theodora will look for

The most common weaknesses in an APPRENTICE-level pedigree:

  • Facts stated without citations (the most common)
  • Dates from death certificates or census records accepted as primary information without qualification
  • Family trees from commercial platforms cited as sources
  • Missing research log — especially missing negative searches
  • Coherence errors not noticed or not addressed
  • No attempt to distinguish primary from secondary information in cited sources

A pedigree that has fewer facts, all correctly sourced and classified, is better than a pedigree with many facts poorly supported. Precision over quantity.

Looking ahead

This capstone marks the completion of the Genealogy APPRENTICE tier. You now have the foundational skills to navigate vital records, census records, church registers, land records, and probate; to use digital platforms critically; to read basic palaeography; to understand naming conventions and historical context; to organise and document research properly; and to recognise and correct common errors. The JUNIOR tier will take you into specialist record sets — military records, regional archives, minority research traditions, and advanced DNA analysis — and will expect you to apply all APPRENTICE skills automatically, as background habits, while developing new specialist capabilities.

storyBeats.text: Theodora clears the table and places two blank forms in front of you — a pedigree chart and a family group sheet. She sets a pen beside each one and stands back.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The moment has arrived. Everything we have discussed — vital records, census schedules, church registers, land deeds, probate, naming conventions, handwriting, historical context, digital tools, research logs, the Genealogical Proof Standard, coherence checks — all of it was preparation for what you are about to do. You are going to document three generations of a real family, with real sources, with every fact cited and every claim classified.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: There is one thing I want you to hold in your mind as you do it. The standard is not perfection. The standard is honesty. A pedigree that admits 'this birth date is secondary information from a death certificate and should be corroborated' is better than a pedigree that presents the same date as established fact. Fewer facts, better evidenced, is always superior to many facts, poorly evidenced. A small, honest, coherent, well-cited pedigree is a contribution to genealogical knowledge. A large, unsourced tree is noise.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: When you have finished — and this work is never truly finished, only submitted — you will look at the three forms and you will see something remarkable. You will see the beginning of a research architecture. The pedigree chart is your map. The family group sheet is your first detailed survey of one square mile of that map. And the research log is the journal of the expedition. The JUNIOR tier begins where this map ends — in the specialist archives, the military records, the regional collections, the advanced DNA analysis. You are ready.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Capstone preparation checklist

Before submitting your pedigree, verify each item:

  • ☐ Pedigree chart completed for three generations (you / parents / grandparents), with all known birth, marriage, and death dates and places
  • ☐ Family group sheet completed for one couple, listing all known children with sources
  • ☐ Every fact has a source citation in the format: record type, repository, specific identifying information, access date
  • ☐ For each cited source, primary or secondary information status is noted
  • ☐ Research log includes all searches conducted (positive and negative), with dates, repositories, search terms, and results
  • ☐ Coherence check passed: all parent-child age gaps are plausible; no death before documented later events; no overlapping sibling births less than 9 months apart
  • ☐ No family trees from commercial platforms cited as sources
  • ☐ Any unresolved gaps or contradictions noted explicitly, not glossed over
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer: This checklist is designed to be self-assessed before submission. Each item maps directly to a skill developed in the APPRENTICE tier: source citation (gen-app-1, gen-app-4 through gen-app-7), primary/secondary classification (gen-app-1, gen-app-1e), research log (gen-app-12), coherence checking (gen-app-14), and critical use of commercial platforms (gen-app-11, gen-app-13). A capstone that passes all checklist items demonstrates full APPRENTICE-tier competency.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏆 Capstone: Your Documented Pedigree

Task

Produce a documented three-generation pedigree meeting the four quality standards below. You may use your own family or an assigned historical family.

Deliverables

  1. Pedigree chart — three generations (yourself or starting person, parents, grandparents). Include all known birth, marriage, and death dates and places. Use question marks for unknowns.
  2. Family group sheet — for one couple in your pedigree (preferably the grandparent generation). Include all known children with birth, marriage, and death information.
  3. Source list — every fact in the pedigree and family group sheet must appear in this list with a full citation: record type, repository, specific identifying information (year, district, volume, page, film number, etc.), and access date for online sources.
  4. Information classification notes — for each major fact (at least one birth date, one marriage date, and one death date), state whether the key information is primary or secondary and explain why.
  5. Research log summary — list at least five searches conducted, including at least two that found nothing. For each entry: date, repository/database, record set, search terms, result.

Assessment criteria

  • Source completeness (25%): all facts cited; no facts presented without supporting evidence
  • Information classification (25%): primary and secondary information correctly distinguished with reasoning
  • Coherence (25%): all dates and relationships internally consistent; contradictions acknowledged and discussed
  • Research log quality (25%): negative searches documented; search terms specified; coverage of plausible record types demonstrated
subChunks.modelAnswer:
This is a performance task — the model answer will vary by family. The following demonstrates what an acceptable submission looks like at APPRENTICE level.

SAMPLE SUBMISSION (abbreviated):

Pedigree: Subject: [Learner]. Father: John Walsh, b. 14 Mar 1948, Dublin, Ireland; m. Mary Murphy, 10 Aug 1970, Dublin; d. 3 Nov 2015, London. Mother: Mary Walsh (née Murphy), b. 22 Jun 1950, Cork, Ireland.

Paternal grandfather: Patrick Walsh, b. ? (c.1915, Ireland), m. Bridget Kelly (c.1940), d. 1978, Dublin.

Source list (sample entries):
- John Walsh birth: Ireland civil birth registration, 14 March 1948, Dublin South registration district; viewed on irishgenealogy.ie, 20 April 2024. [PRIMARY information — registrar was present at the birth report.]
- John Walsh marriage: Ireland civil marriage registration, 10 August 1970, Dublin North; viewed on irishgenealogy.ie, 20 April 2024.
- John Walsh death: England and Wales death registration, November quarter 2015, Hammersmith registration district, vol. W12, p. 44; ordered certificate received March 2024. [PRIMARY for date/place of death; SECONDARY for parents' names, which were provided by a relative from memory.]
- Patrick Walsh birth: Not found. Searched Ireland civil birth registrations 1910–1920 on irishgenealogy.ie for Walsh, Patrick; no entry found for Dublin. Searched Catholic parish registers for Wicklow and Dublin on registers.nli.ie; no Patrick Walsh birth c.1915 found. Date remains approximate.

Research log (sample entries):
- 20 Apr 2024. irishgenealogy.ie. Civil birth registrations, Republic of Ireland, 1944–1955. Search terms: Walsh, John, 1948. Found: John Walsh, 14 March 1948, Dublin South. See citation above.
- 20 Apr 2024. irishgenealogy.ie. Civil birth registrations, Republic of Ireland, 1910–1920. Search terms: Walsh, Patrick. No entry found for Dublin; 11 entries for Patrick Walsh in other counties; none consistent with known facts about Patrick.

Coherence check: All parent-child age gaps plausible. John Walsh born 1948; married 1970 (aged 22) — consistent. Mother Mary born 1950; first child born [year] — check. Patrick Walsh (paternal grandfather) birth date approximate c.1915; would be c.33 at John's birth in 1948 — plausible. No coherence errors identified.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never researched genealogy what it means to 'document' a family tree — and why a tree with five well-cited names is more valuable than one with five hundred uncited ones.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The BCG's five-element framework for proved genealogical conclusions: exhaustive search, accurate citations, evidence analysis, conflict resolution, and soundly reasoned written conclusion.
A standardised form documenting one couple and all their children, with full source citations — the core building block of a documented family tree.
A written narrative explaining how multiple pieces of evidence, including conflicting evidence, combine to support a genealogical conclusion — required by the GPS for complex cases.
The evidence value of a careful, exhaustive search that finds nothing — supporting conclusions about absence of events or records when the search coverage is documented.
The US-based organisation that credentials professional genealogists and publishes the Genealogy Standards manual defining the Genealogical Proof Standard.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is an adequate genealogical source citation?
options: "England and Wales birth registration, June quarter 1872, Aston registration district, vol. 6d, p. 142; image viewed on Ancestry.com, 15 April 2024"
"Family tree built by user JohnSmith1847 on Ancestry"
"Wikipedia article on the Walsh family of Birmingham"
questions.correctAnswer: "England and Wales birth registration, June quarter 1872, Aston registration district, vol. 6d, p. 142; image viewed on Ancestry.com, 15 April 2024"
questions.explanationHtml: An adequate citation gives: record type, repository or database, specific identifying information (year, district, volume and page), and access date for online sources. This citation could be retrieved and checked independently by any researcher. 'Ancestry.com' is a platform, not a source. An Ancestry family tree is an authored work, not a primary or derivative source. A Wikipedia article is an authored tertiary source inappropriate as a genealogical citation.

questions.questionHtml: A death certificate for your great-grandfather states his birthplace as 'County Cork, Ireland' and his birth year as 1845. How should you classify this information and what should you do next?
options: This is secondary information — provided by a relative from memory, not a contemporary record of the birth; you should use it as a working hypothesis and search Irish civil birth registrations and Catholic parish registers for County Cork around 1845 to corroborate or correct it
This is primary information because it is on an official legal document
Birth information on a death certificate is always accurate to within one year
You should accept it as proved and search no further — the death certificate is the best available source
questions.correctAnswer: This is secondary information — provided by a relative from memory, not a contemporary record of the birth; you should use it as a working hypothesis and search Irish civil birth registrations and Catholic parish registers for County Cork around 1845 to corroborate or correct it
questions.explanationHtml: A death certificate is primary information for facts about the death (date, place, cause — reported by the attending doctor). It is secondary information for facts about the deceased's birth and parentage — reported by a relative from memory, often many decades after the event. Ages at death are commonly off by 2–5 years; birthplaces are sometimes wrong county or wrong country. The correct procedure is to treat the death certificate's birth information as a working hypothesis and search for a corroborating primary source — an 1845 Irish civil birth registration (if the area was registered by then) or a Catholic baptism record in County Cork.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher submits a pedigree with 150 ancestors, all copied from an Ancestry family tree built by another user, with no original research and no source citations. A second researcher submits a pedigree with only 8 ancestors across three generations, all supported by primary source citations and a documented research log. Which is the better genealogical product, and why?
options: The 8-ancestor pedigree — it is based on verifiable primary sources and a documented research process; the 150-ancestor pedigree is an authored work without evidence and may contain hundreds of undetected errors
The 150-ancestor pedigree — more information is always more useful
Both are equally valid because they document family history
The 150-ancestor pedigree because it used Ancestry, a professional-grade platform
questions.correctAnswer: The 8-ancestor pedigree — it is based on verifiable primary sources and a documented research process; the 150-ancestor pedigree is an authored work without evidence and may contain hundreds of undetected errors
questions.explanationHtml: Quantity without evidence is not genealogy — it is speculation accumulated without friction. An Ancestry family tree copied from another user is an authored work whose underlying evidence is unknown and whose error rate is unknowable. One error in generation 3 of a copied tree corrupts every generation below it; 150 names copied from an unverified source may represent 5 correct families and 10 strangers, with no way to tell which is which. The 8-ancestor pedigree, by contrast, is a verifiable knowledge claim: every fact can be checked, every conclusion followed. It is smaller but it is real. The standard: fewer facts, better evidenced, is always superior. This principle is the foundation of the Genealogical Proof Standard and the most important habit the APPRENTICE tier develops.
